alternatives: NSAID at headache onset (naproxen 500 mg or ibuprofen 400-600 mg) with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg).
Gepants (rimegepant, ubrogepant) or lasmiditan are not vasoconstrictive; data in hemiplegic migraine are limited.
contraindications: Triptans: the product labels (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) exclude use in hemiplegic and basilar-type migraine because no safety data exist in these patients; small retrospective series have reported no vascular events, but the label restriction stands.
Ergotamine and dihydroergotamine: avoid in hemiplegic migraine (vasoconstriction); never within 24 h of a triptan.
output.formulary_status: Naproxen, ibuprofen, metoclopramide and domperidone on formulary; gepants and lasmiditan restricted.
interactions: Lomerizine (calcium-channel blocker): no pharmacokinetic interaction with triptans or NSAIDs; additive blood-pressure lowering with other antihypertensives.
Meloxicam: no interaction with triptans; do not combine with a second NSAID (additive gastrointestinal bleeding and renal risk).
Diazepam: no interaction with triptans or NSAIDs; additive sedation with alcohol, opioids or sedating antiemetics.
output.proposed: Triptan (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, zolmitriptan) or ergot derivative for acute attacks
output.summary: Triptans and ergot derivatives fall outside their licensed use in hemiplegic migraine; no clinically relevant interaction among the current medicines. Sources: sumatriptan, rizatriptan and zolmitriptan SmPC and US prescribing information; AHS consensus statement 2021 (Ailani J et al., Headache 2021;61:1021-1039).
warnings: Traditional herbal medicine of unknown composition: identify the product; ephedra (ma huang)-containing preparations are sympathomimetic and vasoconstrictive, and liquorice-containing preparations can raise blood pressure and lower potassium.
Metoclopramide: extrapyramidal reactions; maximum 30 mg a day for up to 5 days.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Two attacks of reversible right-sided motor and sensory aura with gradual spread and following headache meet ICHD-3 1.2.3; no affected relative (sporadic); red flags: motor aura and impaired consciousness
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with neurological examination and red-flag review, applying the ICHD-3 1.2.3 hemiplegic migraine criteria explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: Hemiplegic migraine is a clinical diagnosis: ICHD-3 1.2.3 requires two attacks of fully reversible motor aura with visual, sensory or speech aura, and the sporadic form requires no affected first- or second-degree relative. The history also identifies the red flags (motor aura, impaired consciousness) that justify imaging.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, haemorrhage or structural lesion in the left hemisphere or elsewhere
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI: a first motor aura with impaired consciousness is a red flag for imaging
action_criteria.rationale: Motor aura and impaired consciousness are red flags (AHS neuroimaging evidence assessment, Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336). MRI excludes infarction and structural mimics; a normal DWI excludes infarction but not TIA, so the distinction from TIA remains clinical. MRI does not establish migraine.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal intracranial and cervical arteries: no dissection, stenosis, aneurysm or vascular malformation
action_criteria.label: Obtain MR angiography of the head and neck to exclude arterial dissection, stenosis or a vascular malformation at first presentation of motor aura
action_criteria.rationale: Recurrent transient hemiparesis with headache at first presentation raises cervical artery dissection, intracranial stenosis and vascular malformation; MRA answers this as a separate study from the brain MRI.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Gene panel result; a negative panel does not exclude hemiplegic migraine
action_criteria.label: Optional: hemiplegic migraine gene panel (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A, PRRT2)
action_criteria.rationale: Adult-onset sporadic hemiplegic migraine with two attacks: testing may be offered, but the yield is low and the result does not change management today [ICHD_3] (Di Stefano V et al., Diagnostic and therapeutic aspects of hemiplegic migraine, J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2020;91:764-771).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Acute treatment must avoid the vasoconstrictor classes whose labels exclude hemiplegic migraine; the current medicines raise no interaction
action_criteria.label: Check the acute-treatment options against hemiplegic migraine and the current medicines before prescribing
action_criteria.rationale: Triptan and ergot labels exclude hemiplegic migraine (no safety data), which changes the acute plan; the check also covers his lomerizine, meloxicam, diazepam and herbal medicine. Sources: triptan SmPC and US prescribing information; AHS consensus statement 2021 (Ailani J et al., Headache 2021;61:1021-1039).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on the diagnosis and acute treatment of hemiplegic migraine
action_criteria.label: Optionally consult the literature on hemiplegic migraine criteria and acute treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe triptans or ergot derivatives for acute attacks of hemiplegic migraine.

Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for presumed TIA: the episodes have the features of migraine aura (motor and sensory symptoms spreading over 20-25 minutes, followed by headache, in two stereotyped attacks) and imaging shows no infarct.
required_recommendations: Do not use a triptan or ergot derivative for attacks; treat attacks at headache onset with one NSAID (for example naproxen 500 mg or ibuprofen 400-600 mg, not together with his meloxicam) plus an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg).

Review prevention: two hemiplegic attacks within 3 weeks on lomerizine 10 mg daily justify optimising or changing the preventive; options in hemiplegic migraine are verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide or lamotrigine (case series and expert opinion, no randomised trials), with topiramate as an alternative.
Offer referral to clinical genetics for hemiplegic migraine gene testing (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A, PRRT2); the yield is lower in sporadic adult-onset cases.
Advise emergency stroke assessment if weakness starts suddenly rather than spreading over minutes, differs from the previous attacks, or does not resolve.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve it for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT or for meningitis, neither of which is present here.
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in the MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM trials.

accepted: Sporadic hemiplegic migraine (ICHD-3 1.2.3) — two qualifying episodes with gradual motor and sensory aura followed by headache; all secondary causes excluded

differential.key_features: Against: motor and sensory symptoms built up over 20-25 min, were followed by headache and recurred in a stereotyped form; age 39 without vascular risk factors; MRI shows no infarct and MRA no arterial lesion. A normal DWI excludes infarction, not TIA: the distinction rests on these clinical features.
No first- or second-degree relative with hemiplegic attacks; genetic testing is a referral decision, not needed for the sporadic diagnosis.
No neck pain or trauma; MRA shows no dissection.

differential.diagnosis: Focal motor seizure with postictal (Todd) paresis
differential.key_features: Raised by the unresponsiveness in attack 2. Against: weakness spread over 20-25 min rather than a march over seconds, no clonic activity described, headache followed, and impaired consciousness is a recognised feature of severe hemiplegic migraine attacks.
Unresponsiveness followed a motor aura that had evolved over minutes and was followed by headache; regular pulse, normal cardiac examination, no cardiac history.
No short stature, hearing loss, diabetes, myopathy or maternal family history; attacks fully reversible and MRI normal.

key_clinical_evidence: Two attacks of fully reversible right-sided motor and sensory aura spreading over 20-25 min and followed by left occipital headache meet ICHD-3 1.2.3; no affected first- or second-degree relative, so sporadic (1.2.3.2)

Motor aura and impaired consciousness are red flags for imaging: brain MRI excludes infarction and structural causes, MRA excludes dissection and other arterial lesions; a normal DWI excludes infarction, not TIA
Decreased consciousness during the second attack is compatible with hemiplegic migraine
Triptan and ergot labels exclude hemiplegic migraine; acute treatment is an NSAID with an antiemetic

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Weakness with sensory symptoms that spread over 20-25 min and were followed by headache, in two stereotyped attacks at 39 without vascular risk factors, is hemiplegic migraine; imaging shows no infarct or arterial lesion
red_herrings.data_point: Right-sided limb weakness in a 39-year-old man

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Impaired consciousness occurs in severe hemiplegic migraine attacks; the gradual spread of the motor and sensory aura and the headache on recovery point to migraine rather than a seizure with postictal paresis or cardiac syncope
red_herrings.data_point: Found unresponsive by a colleague during the second episode
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt a seizure or syncope diagnosis and an EEG or cardiac work-up

sequence_constraints.reason: The history identifies the red flags (motor aura, impaired consciousness) that justify imaging.

findings.result: Two stereotyped attacks, 20 days and 2 days before this visit. Earlier intermittent headaches without motor symptoms.

Motor: weakness of the right arm and leg in both attacks. Sensory: tense, numb feeling of the right face (attack 1) and right perioral area (attack 2); sensory disturbance over the ulnar aspect of the right upper arm (attack 2).
Weakness and sensory symptoms built up gradually over 20-25 min (attack 1).
Motor and sensory symptoms began together; no sequential order of aura symptoms described.
Attack 1: aura resolved over 30-40 min after the build-up. Attack 2: motor and sensory symptoms improved over several hours (motor within 72 h; the sensory symptom exceeded 60 min).
All aura symptoms right-sided; headache left occipital in both attacks.
Tense facial and perioral dysaesthesia (positive sensory symptom) with numbness.
Left occipital headache after the aura in attack 1 and on recovery of consciousness in attack 2, within 60 min; the first relieved by meloxicam.
Attack 2: found unresponsive by a colleague; regained consciousness during ambulance transfer. Attack 1: no loss of consciousness.
No first- or second-degree relative with hemiplegic attacks; mother had occasional headaches.
Headache-free. Normal mental status, cranial nerves, power, tone, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. BP 139/91 mmHg, pulse 70 regular.

Neurological deficit during attacks (motor aura): present. Impaired consciousness (attack 2): present. New aura type (first motor aura): present. Systemic symptoms, fever, cancer history: absent. Sudden (thunderclap) onset: absent, onset built up over 20-25 min. Onset after 50: absent (age 39). Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Pregnancy: not applicable. Neurological deficit on examination today: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: 1. Two attacks of fully reversible right-sided motor and sensory aura with gradual spread, followed by left occipital headache: meets ICHD-3 1.2.3 hemiplegic migraine (criterion C 3 of 4; 1.2 criterion C 4 of 6). No affected first- or second-degree relative (sporadic form, 1.2.3.2). 2. Red flags: motor aura, impaired consciousness in attack 2, new aura type. 3. Normal neurological examination today; no sudden onset, no seizure features described.

mri.impression: Normal MRI brain. No acute or chronic infarct, haemorrhage or structural lesion.

patient.chief_complaint: Two episodes of right-sided limb weakness with left occipital headache over the past 3 weeks — sent for urgent evaluation

family_history: No family history of hemiplegic migraine, stroke, or coagulopathy; mother had occasional headaches; no MELAS family history

patient.history_present_illness:
A 39-year-old Japanese man with a long-standing history of myofascial pain syndrome and intermittent headaches was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic for urgent evaluation after two episodes of transient right-sided limb weakness. The first episode occurred 20 days prior to this visit: he noticed weakness in his right arm and right leg while at home, along with a tense, numb feeling on the right side of his face. These symptoms developed gradually over approximately 20-25 minutes and resolved over the following 30-40 minutes. Afterwards, he experienced a left occipital headache that he treated with meloxicam with good relief.

The second episode occurred 2 days before this visit. He was at work when he again developed right upper and lower limb weakness and a tense feeling on the right side of his mouth. He was found unresponsive by a colleague and transported by ambulance to a local emergency department. En route to hospital, he regained consciousness and complained of a left occipital headache. At the emergency department, he was alert with right limb weakness and sensory disturbance over the ulnar aspect of the right upper arm. He was admitted for observation. His symptoms gradually improved over several hours and he was discharged with an outpatient referral when no acute cause was identified.

He has a history of migraine headaches and myofascial pain, managed with lomerizine hydrochloride and as-needed NSAIDs. He has no prior stroke, no hypertension, no diabetes, and no cardiac disease. He is a non-smoker. He reports no family history of hemiplegic migraine. He is now headache-free and fully neurologically intact at this consultation.
